output.title: Design against positioning drift with one workflow check
output.body:
If you want to design against positioning drift, make it one bounded workflow decision: define the one customer problem or outcome your business says it consistently solves. That is your positioning anchor. Everything else should be checked against it.

For a small business, the question is not whether you can write better copy. It is whether your current workflow keeps sending mixed signals. Pick one repeatable place where drift shows up: how you triage customer inquiries, how you answer sales questions, or how you negotiate project scope. Choose the one that creates confusion most often.

Write the anchor in plain English, then use it as a manual check in that workflow for a short period. If the same questions keep coming up, or scope keeps expanding in ways that pull you off-message, you have found a real control point. If the workflow stays consistent, the anchor is probably doing its job.

AI can help later by enforcing that wording inside documents, email, CRM, or back-office workflows, but only after you have confirmed the anchor is actually right. The knowledge assistant and workflow automation Bareni has built are self-built demos, not customer-validated systems, so this is still an owner decision first. Final approval stays human. That is the useful part, even if it is not very dramatic.

Which workflow in your business surfaces positioning ambiguity most often? Start there, because it is usually the cheapest place to test the anchor first.
